profiled_workloads.selection_reason: float16 [1024] = 1024 elements, 4096 B total logical traffic; the seed's tile rule resolves this to BLOCK=1024, unmasked clamp kernel, grid=1 program, so it isolates per-call overhead almost completely and any latency there cannot be data movement.

float16 [1048576] = 1,048,576 elements, 4,194,304 B traffic, different tile (BLOCK=16384, grid=64). Boundary probe for the flat-floor regime: 1024x the elements of timing-0, so unchanged latency places the marginal device cost of 4 MB below measurement noise.

float32 [1024] control for the small-case floor with a different dtype and a different kernel branch: fp32 takes the fp32-staged compare/select path (BLOCK=8192), so latency equal to fp16 timing-0 shows the floor is branch-independent.

float16 [4096,4096] = 16,777,216 elements, 67,108,864 B logical. Worst speedup of the round (0.5313, recorded as worst_workload_uuid) and largest absolute gap (27.0 us); profiled twice because the first attempt was part of a 6-workload batch.

bfloat16 [4096,4096]. Paired discriminator against timing-3: identical elements, width, logical bytes and kernel/tile selection (element_size==2 -> native clamp, BLOCK=16384), yet 1.46x slower, which isolates dtype codegen from data volume.

float32 [4096,4096]. Largest logical traffic in the set (134,217,728 B) and the only regime where one direction (67 MiB) is a substantial fraction of the 168 MiB L2, testing whether the large-case limit is HBM streaming or cache/codegen organization.

performance_interpretation: NO DEVICE COUNTERS EXIST FOR THIS ROUND (see error and warnings); every number below is arithmetic over the authoritative round-1 walltime eval latencies plus facts from the frozen workload specs, and is explicitly not a measured hardware metric. Authoritative state: geo_mean 0.7142152693274566, 30/30 PASSED, worst_workload_uuid nan_to_num_-timing-3, solution_sha256 2aaa7508bbeb4de745106d3987e0152b0b479ee47ae194eea7a9149c89f576bf. TWO REGIMES. (1) Nine of twelve timing workloads sit in a flat band: timing-0 16.912, timing-1 16.623, timing-2 16.597, timing-4 15.927, timing-5 16.103, timing-6 16.182, timing-8 16.423, timing-9 16.223, timing-10 15.859 us - mean 16.3165 us with a total spread of only 1.053 us - while element count spans 1024 to 1,048,576 and logical traffic spans 4096 B to 8,388,608 B, a 2048x range with no trend. Multiplying elements by 1024 (timing-0 -> timing-2) changes latency by -0.32 us (inside noise), and the 8.39 MB fp32 case timing-10 is the fastest of the nine at 15.859 us. timing-0's own tile rule resolves to grid=1 program over 1024 elements, so its 16.912 us contains essentially no data movement. A work-proportional cost therefore cannot be hiding under the floor: the marginal cost of up to 8.4 MB is below this measurement's noise. The reference over the same nine is 10.908-14.139 us (mean 12.0640), i.e. the candidate carries a fixed-cost penalty of 4.2525 us (1.352x). GEO_MEAN LEVERAGE: these nine hold nine of the twelve factors. Removing their gap entirely would multiply geo_mean by (1/0.06420)^(1/12) = 1.257 to about 0.898; recovering 3 us of the 4.25 us gives roughly 0.82-0.83. Lifting all three large cases to ratio 0.75 is worth only about 1.037 (0.714 -> 0.740). So the dominant lever is per-call fixed cost, not large-case device work, and no tile/byte change can move the nine. The remaining ambiguity - how that 16.3 us splits into python/dispatch, launch/driver, device kernel latency and measurement floor - is exactly what msprof failed to measure. (2) The 4096x4096 cases are a separate device-work regime: timing-3 float16 [4096,4096] 16,777,216 elements, 67,108,864 B logical, 57.588 us, ratio 0.5313 (round minimum, gap 27.0 us); timing-7 bfloat16 same shape/bytes, 84.038 us, ratio 0.7386 (gap 22.0 us); timing-11 float32 [4096,4096] 16,777,216 elements, 134,217,728 B logical, 83.596 us, ratio 0.6992 (gap 25.2 us). Inside this regime timing-3 versus timing-7 is the cleanest natural experiment available: same 16,777,216 elements, same 2-byte width, same 67,108,864 logical bytes, same seed kernel and same BLOCK=16384 tile (both take the native-dtype clamp because element_size()==2), yet 26.45 us apart (1.459x). Volume, element count and grid shape are excluded, leaving dtype-specific lowering - plausibly bfloat16 tl.maximum/tl.minimum not being native vector max/min and being lowered through float32 - as a hypothesis to test, NOT a measured fact. The reference shows the same direction (torch bf16 62.071 vs fp16 30.597 us, 2.03x), but the candidate is 1.88x the reference on fp16 versus only 1.35x on bf16, so fp16 timing-3 is the single largest large-case opportunity. Bandwidth framing is NOT supported: apparent logical rates of 1165 GB/s (timing-3), 798 GB/s (timing-7) and 1606 GB/s (timing-11), or 1626 and 1995 GB/s net of a 16.32 us fixed floor for timing-3 and timing-11, are too high to accept as HBM streaming for a 33.5-67 MiB buffer that fits inside the target's 176,160,768 B (168 MiB) L2 and is re-touched over 110 iterations - and they are mutually inconsistent, since timing-7 moves the same bytes as timing-3 at the same tile while being 1.46x slower. So HBM saturation is unestablished and a bandwidth-only rewrite (bigger tiles, fewer programs) should not be expected to close timing-3's 27 us gap. Integrity check: the seed header claims 58.5 us for the fp16 native clamp versus 84.4 us for the fp32-staged compare/select on this shape; the measured 57.588 us for timing-3 agrees, supporting that the intended native-clamp branch is the one actually running and that the fp16/bf16 split is not a dispatch accident.

next_experiment.action_description: Reduce per-call fixed cost on the contiguous default-parameter path only; do not touch device tiles, kernel bodies, the strided/8D path or the legacy fallback. Collapse run() and _dispatch() so that, after the first call for a given (dtype, numel, device) key, the stored plan is a single prebuilt closure holding (launch callable, ck.function, ck.packed_metadata, precomputed grid tuple, stream getter), and the hot path performs only: one dict get, one current-stream read, and one launch call carrying (pointer, n, nan, posinf, neginf). Concretely, move onto the build path everything currently recomputed per call - A.is_contiguous(), A.get_device(), the dtype/element-size re-derivation, triton.cdiv(n, block) grid computation, the 6-tuple plan rebuild and the entry[0](entry[3], 1, 1, ...) argument assembly - while keeping those checks unconditional on the first call for each key and on every key miss. The current-stream handle MUST still be read on every call, because the evaluator switches streams. Keep the existing guard that falls back to _legacy_run when launcher.compile_only or launcher.enable_msprof_register_tensor is set, so a later profiling-capable round does not silently profile the wrong branch.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Conditional and deliberately falsifiable. If the 4.25 us gap over the reference floor is python/dispatch work inside run(), the nine <=1M-element timing workloads move from mean 16.3165 us to roughly 13.0-14.5 us (mean ratio 0.738 -> 0.85-0.92), multiplying geo_mean by ~1.10-1.16 from 0.7142 to about 0.79-0.83. If instead the floor is intrinsic triton/CANN launch latency on this stack, the change buys less than 1 us and the hypothesis is refuted by the same measurement - that negative result is itself the deliverable, because it redirects round 3 to the device regime where timing-3 and timing-7 diverge at equal bytes. The three 4096x4096 cases are expected to be essentially untouched, since a ~4 us fixed cost is small against 58-84 us.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risks: (a) stream correctness - caching a stream handle instead of reading the current stream per call would break the evaluator's stream switching, so the per-call read must stay; (b) dropping A.is_contiguous() or the pointer-alignment check from the hot path would send a non-contiguous or misaligned tensor into the contiguous kernel and write the wrong real storage slots, violating the in-place contract that the six strided correctness workloads protect; (c) plan keys must stay unique per (dtype, numel, device) because the plan cache is a process-global; (d) in-place identity must be preserved - same tensor object, same storage mutated, A returned. Rollback is a single-file restore of main.py to solution_sha256 2aaa7508bbeb4de745106d3987e0152b0b479ee47ae194eea7a9149c89f576bf (round-1 candidate, geo_mean 0.7142152693274566, 30/30 PASSED, .kernelgen/evals/round-0001/main.py). The change is confined to the host wrapper, so rollback leaves no stale device state or compiled-artifact mismatch.

Because the artifact registry for round 1 is empty, findings and their evidence could not be validated by record_profile_analysis; the analysis is therefore carried in performance_interpretation, open_questions and this warnings list, and it is flagged as eval-derived arithmetic rather than profiler fact. The manifests still record the profiled target's L2 size (176,160,768 B) and collection options (warmup 10, iterations 100) as configuration facts.

The collector ran with warmup 10 and iterations 100, and the candidate source itself refuses its direct compiled launch when launcher.enable_msprof_register_tensor is set; a successful collection would therefore have profiled the _legacy_run fallback branch rather than the production fast path. Any future profiling round must account for this branch switch before attributing device numbers to the production path.

All latency figures are walltime per call (the eval result records timing=walltime), so they include host dispatch and cannot separate host from device without counters. No physical HBM bytes were measured; every GB/s figure in this analysis is logical bytes divided by eval latency and must not be quoted as achieved bandwidth.

The scheduler still carries a historical incident string about an isolated evaluate worker crashing with exitcode=-11 on npu:0 (13 incidents, 13 recovered, slot currently available). open_questions: What is the measured device kernel duration for timing-0 (grid=1, 1024 fp16 elements) versus timing-2 (grid=64, 1,048,576 elements)? If both are ~2-3 us then 13-14 us of the 16.3 us floor is host/launch and host slimming is well targeted; if timing-0 is already ~14 us, the floor is intrinsic launch latency and only the large cases are worth attacking. msprof could not answer this in round 1.

Does the bfloat16 clamp lower through float32 conversions for tl.maximum/tl.minimum, or is the 1.46x penalty from address/compute scheduling? Settling this needs the instruction listing msprof failed to produce; an instruction-level request on timing-3 and timing-7 is the cheapest route once collection works.

Why does the reference itself cost 30.597 us for fp16 4096x4096 but 62.071 us for the identical-byte bfloat16 case? If the reference fp16 path is a markedly lighter instruction sequence, that is the shape of timing-3's 27.0 us gap and sets the realistic target for the large cases.

Would this stack accept a 2-byte tile larger than BLOCK=16384 without UB overflow, and could it matter at all given that a ~4 us scale change is absorbed by the fixed floor? The seed notes UB overflow above 32 KiB of staging, so a 64 KiB 2-byte tile is speculative and should only be attempted after the launch-path question is answered.
